React Router 🌐

React Router is the standard library for implementing client-side routing in React applications, enabling them to function as Single Page Applications (SPAs). It allows the user interface (UI) to stay in sync with the browser URL without requiring a full page reload. This is achieved through declarative route definitions and efficient management of the browser's history object.

Key Components of React Router

  • Router: The core component that enables routing. You must wrap your entire application (or a specific section) within one of the router types such as BrowserRouter, HashRouter, or MemoryRouter.

Why Use React Router?

  • Provides seamless page transitions without full reloads, improving performance and user experience.
  • Supports dynamic routing—routes can be created based on app state or user data.
  • Keeps UI and URL perfectly synchronized for better navigation and SEO handling.
  • Offers built-in components and hooks for programmatic navigation, nested routes, and route protection.

Types of Routers in React Router

React Router provides several router components built on top of the core history library. The choice depends on your deployment environment and application needs.

  • 1. BrowserRouter (Recommended)
    • Mechanism: Uses the HTML5 History API (pushState, replaceState) to keep the UI in sync with the URL.
    • URL Style: Provides clean URLs, e.g., http://example.com/about.
    • When to Use: Ideal for modern web apps where the server can serve index.html for any route, letting React handle client-side routing.
    
import { BrowserRouter } from 'react-router-dom';
  • 2. HashRouter
    • Mechanism: Uses the hash portion of the URL (after #) to manage routing. The hash part isn't sent to the server.
    • URL Style: Includes a hash symbol, e.g., http://example.com/#/about.
    • When to Use: Perfect for static file servers that can’t handle dynamic routes or older browser environments.
    
import { HashRouter } from 'react-router-dom';
  • 3. MemoryRouter
    • Mechanism: Keeps navigation history entirely in memory and doesn’t affect the browser’s address bar.
    • URL Style: No visible URL changes in the browser.
    • When to Use: Commonly used for testing, React Native, or server-side rendering (SSR) where no browser history is available.
    
import { MemoryRouter } from 'react-router-dom';

React Router vs. DOM History API

React Router abstracts the lower-level DOM History API (like window.history.pushState() and popstate events) into declarative, component-based routing. With hooks such as useNavigate, developers can easily manage navigation within React's lifecycle instead of manually manipulating the global window.history object.

Navigation Using useNavigate() Hook

The useNavigate() hook allows programmatic navigation from within components (e.g., after form submission).


import { useNavigate } from 'react-router-dom';

function Login() {
  const navigate = useNavigate();

  const handleLogin = () => {
    // Perform login validation
    navigate('/dashboard'); // Redirect after login
  };

  return ;
}

Protected Routes (Private Routing)

A Protected Route ensures that only authenticated users can access specific pages.
